stories.title: Kemi Badenoch has cemented her image. Now she wants to put her party back on the big stage
stories.summary: The Conservative leader is expected to set out a return to core conservative principles at the party’s annual conference.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Kemi Badenoch has cemented her image. Now she wants to put her party back on the big stage

Published 3 October 2026, 11:27 BST

The 2026 Conservative conference is big enough to justify using Birmingham's Symphony Hall as its main stage again.

So, Kemi Badenoch will tread the same stage ageing rockers Marillion took last month - and where sequinned soprano Katherine Jenkins will perform next week. She'll also avoid the humiliation of a national party leader being squashed into a side room at a corporate conference centre (with drapes portioning off the empty space). Simply, the party is able to put bums on seats again - and by that measure, things are looking up.

Badenoch goes into the conference with her own position secure in the party. One senior Tory says "she has actually defied cynics like me" who initially disapproved of her leadership. Her standing with the public has improved and she is now, again on a very simple but crucial measure, much better known. Her allies are sure she has developed a clear identity among the public, confiding: "People now know who she is and they enjoy her interventions - the thing we hear most is I don't always agree with her but I know where she stands."

But Conservative MPs are aware that the party itself still has a much bigger issue - in the words of one shadow cabinet member: "The problem we still have is trust of the party and the brand". The shadow of the years of chaos still looms. And while Badenoch has made good progress since she took the job, most of that was up against an unpopular prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, on whom she landed plenty of political punches. She has to show "what being Conservative is now", says another senior Tory, taking on a different, more popular, rival in Andy Burnham.

The Tories' warm-up to conference has been so far, so traditional. A proposed dramatic expansion of prison places kicks off Badenoch's second big party get-together. With it, a message that echoes the well-known mantra of the early 1990s Tories, issued by former leader Michael Howard at party conference: "Prison works". They are not just talking about adding on a few cells here and there, but spelling out a monumental increase in the numbers of people that the country locks up.

That follows the announcement of a new "tough love" approach for young people trying to claim benefits. Don't expect the shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whateley, to produce a moment as controversial as when the then-welfare secretary, Peter Lilley, proclaimed from the stage that he had "a little list" of benefit claimants he wanted to root out. But the Conservatives are determined to keep concentrating on the size of the welfare bill – believing it's right to do so for financial and moral reasons.

You can expect to hear more in the week about fundamental conservative principles: people keeping more of their own money, government only stepping in when really required to, pointed concern about the level of the country's debt and public spending. And again, of course, that means Kemi Badenoch disavowing much of what the Conservatives did in office between 2010 and 2024, when the civil service grew, the tax burden grew, a law was passed to try to combat climate change, the list goes on.

She'll set out at some length in the coming days what she sees as classic conservative first principles: the core beliefs the party was founded on and drifted from, she reckons, in the years gone by. If anything, Badenoch told interviewers this week the party was "finally saying what we believe" and "should be more aggressive" in displaying the party's core.

The frontbench at last year's Conservative conference

She believes the arrival of Andy Burnham makes that easier. There's a clearer contrast between the two. A senior ally of Badenoch says Burnham has "opened the door to it quite well, as he has harked back to the '70s in a way that I'm astonished by". Suggesting the pleasing atmospherics of Burnham's Labour are just that, atmospherics, the ally adds: "It's like a fairy story where he has come to the rescue of Britain and he has a wand in his hand and nothing else".

As we talked about a couple of weeks ago , the contrasts between Labour and the Conservatives are sharper now Burnham is in post, and the conference season is only serving to exaggerate that. They are both only too happy to emphasise it with their messages, retro or not, designed to show the true souls of their tribes.

But while Badenoch might find it easier to argue clearly with Burnham, rather than tangle with Starmer over process, it is harder to face an opponent who, at least for now, is proving more appealing to the public. And while plenty of Conservatives are hopeful in private that Reform might have peaked, they can't be sure that's true, or that the swathes of voters who abandoned the Tories for Farage's party will return.

Badenoch has always seemed allergic to the idea of doing any kind of deal with Reform, who she dismisses as a party of protest. And her allies hope, and some believe, that Reform's appeal will fade, making the Conservatives again the obvious alternative government. But fundamental arithmetic displays that, for as long as millions of voters on the right are tempted by Farage, it's harder for the Tories to triumph. One shadow minister admits "we've still got a whole battle on the right" even though "Kemi's boldness" is beginning to break through.

So, in the coming next days, prepare for a "classic showing of Tory wares": an attempt by the party's leader to set out their fundamental beliefs about the country and how it should be governed.

There are pockets of nerves that Kemi Badenoch risks rewinding to an previous era. One when another newly confident leader, David Cameron, ushered in the modern Tory party on the conference stage in front of digitally produced green foliage and sunlight. One former cabinet minister warns that it's "the big risk – so easy to slip into an alienating divisive manner – nasty party stuff".

When it comes to policy, and striking the right tone, they warn that Badenoch must "be mindful that she has to win Cheltenham and Maidenhead as well as Clacton".

But Kemi Badenoch is visibly more confident and is aware of the chance in front of her – seemingly unworried about the possible downsides of making an increasingly direct argument to you, eager to stride that mercifully bigger Birmingham stage.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Joshua Kerry has been charged with preparing acts of terror including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Published 2 October 2026

The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has also been charged with preparing acts of terror including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Counter terror police said Joshua Kerry, 28, was charged on Friday with one count of preparation of terrorist acts.

The charge relates to activity which is alleged to have taken place between May 2024 and July 2026.

Kerry was charged in July with the murder of 78-year-old Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said she knew the fresh charge would be "extremely concerning" and her "profound sympathies" were with Farage and his family.

"Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all.

"This case raises serious questions about the security of those in public life. We must use this as an opportunity to reset. Once parliament returns, I will update on our work to strengthen protections for those who choose to serve."

The BBC contacted Reform UK for comment and a party source said: "This is exactly why Nigel needed £5m to protect his security for life."

Farage is currently facing a parliamentary standards watchdog probe into a £5m gift from a billionaire donor before he returned as an MP in 2024. The Reform leader has previously said the money was for his personal security.

Ann Widdecombe's murder 'a wake-up call' - Reform UK deputy leader

Deputy leader of Reform UK, Richard Tice, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the murder of Ann Widdecombe had made everyone take security more seriously.

"What's particularly upsetting for those of us in and around him [Farage] is sometimes he's not been believed, not been listened to."

Tice added that he personally had security arrangements in place and his habits had changed which was a "consequence of the world we live in" arguing the "online world has clearly hindered this whole process".

Asked if Reform had done enough to dial the temperature down and whether comments from politicians added to public anger, Tice said "the passions that flow through democratic debate should be completely separate to the way that people respond

"It's the nature of democracy... it's part of the joy of it is that there will be robust debate but at the end of it one should be able to shake hands."

Counter Terrorism Policing Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said the charge on Friday was the result of a "hugely intensive and complex investigation".

"This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts, and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of enquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge," she added.

Kerry, from Rotherham, is due to appear in court over the terror charge on Wednesday, police said.

Frank Ferguson of the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division said prosecutors "worked closely" with police to bring the charge and would continue to work alongside them as the investigation continued.

Widdecombe was found dead on Thursday 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.

She served as Conservative MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

Following her departure from the Commons, Widdecombe appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing and would later become a Reform UK spokeswoman.

Polanski calls for 'national fair rent guarantee'

Published 2 October 2026

Zack Polanski has urged voters to back the Greens to force changes from Andy Burnham, arguing his party has the power to move Labour in "the right direction".

In his speech to the party's annual conference, the Green leader said that "sustained pressure" from his party had made forced Labour into changing its stance on issues including climate and its stance towards Israel.

He told activists in Brighton that Labour had failed to take action on housing, as he called for a three-year cap to limit rent rises in the private sector.

And he said that voting for the Greens would force changes from the government, telling members: "Vote Green, and watch Labour move".

Polanski arrived in Brighton facing questions over his leadership of the party amid signs the Greens' rise in popularity last year may have waned, and how he would respond to Labour's change of leadership under Burnham.

In his half-hour address, he did not mention the Conservatives or Reform UK but launched repeated attacks on Labour's record in office.

He criticised Labour for making "slogans without action" on the cost of living and vowed only his party would end "Rip Off Britain".

And he was particularly critical of Labour's record on housing, where he accused the party of failing to take on the "powerful vested interests of developers and big landlords".

Instead, he urged the government to enact an "emergency brake" on private rents, under which they would be prevented from rising above the lowest of consumer price index measure of inflation, wage growth or 2%, for three years.

'Sustained pressure'

He argued that pressure from the Greens in the face of government "inaction" had forced Burnham into calling an emergency Cobr meeting this summer amid record-breaking hot and dry temperatures.

The Greens, he added would not "hesitate" to tax "extreme wealth", as he repeated the party's call for a so-called windfall tax on back profits - an issue where the government has faced pressure from unions.

"Through our sustained pressure – and our historic wins – we have held the worst instincts of the Labour government in check.

"And we have started to move them in the right direction. But we can't wait for them to get there on their own."

He also sought to draw a clear dividing line with the government on the issue of oil and gas, ahead of looming decisions for the government on whether to approve the Rosebank oil field and Jackdaw gas field.

Burnham has stuck to Labour's manifesto commitment not to issue new oil and gas licences, but has left open the possibility of approving the two sites.

This summer's wildfires, Polanski told the conference hall, should prove the "final nail in the coffin for new oil and gas".

Zionism motion

He began his address by celebrating his party's surge in membership since his election as party leader a year ago, and electoral successes including the hundreds of councillors it gained in May's local elections in England .

But his speech did not touch on an issue that could divide the membership over the weekend, ahead of a probable vote on a motion put forward by members that describes Zionism as a form of racism.

The motion defines Zionism as an ideology in support of "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and seeks to shift the party's position to supporting a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".

The current form of the motion has drawn criticism from senior figures, including deputy leader Rachel Millward, who earlier described it as "problematic".

Former leader Caroline Lucas told the BBC: "I think there is no single definition of Zionism and, irrespective of the intentions of those who put that motion, I think there is a real risk that it will be divisive and could be seen as a sign that Jewish people aren't welcome in the party."

It has also attracted criticism from some Jewish groups including the Board of Deputies and the Jewish Leadership Council.

Green MP Sian Berry would not confirm how she planned to vote on the motion but said she could "absolutely see and feel how strongly many members feel we should be saying even more".

Under Green Party rules if the motion passes it would officially become party policy, but would not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto.

Polanski has said he wants to see the motion amended to specify that it should not be used to discipline Jewish members attending synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.

He is also supporting a change that would replace the call for a single Palestinian state with backing for a "lasting settlement granting equal rights for all" to be "shaped and determined by Palestinians themselves".

Asked by the BBC if he believed that Zionism is racism, Polanski said it would depend on how the term was defined.

"If your Zionism is the displacement of the Palestinian people then that is clearly racist, and I say that as a Jewish leader of a British political party."

Asked whether the conference motion was calling for the eradication of Israel, Polanski said: "That's why I'm calling for an amendment."

"I don't believe we as a Green Party of England and Wales or even the British government should be deciding what the future settlement looks like," he added.

When asked if he believed Israel had a right to exist, Polanski said: "I believe people have a right to exist."

Asked the same question again, he said: "Both Israelis have a right to exist and Palestinians have a right to exist."

Pushed for a third time on whether Israel had a right to exist, he said: "Our job as political parties is to defend the rights of people, not the rights of nations."

Polanski also said he wanted to focus on what the party could "materially do to make a difference" such as campaigning for the UK government to stop selling arms to Israel and sharing intelligence with the Israeli government.

stories.body:
Exclusive: Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith told party members last year he had discussed making further savings if they win next election

The Conservatives are planning to make sweeping cuts beyond the £47bn announced last year if they win the next election, according to leaked comments by the shadow chancellor.

Speaking last year when he was shadow business secretary, Andrew Griffith told Conservative members he and fellow shadow cabinet ministers had discussed making further cuts in “every part of government”.

The comments, which have emerged on the eve of the Tory party conference in Birmingham, suggested that the Conservatives are planning to make cuts similar in scale to those made during the austerity years should they take power.

Last October, Griffith said: “There are decisions made and signed up to by everybody to deliver that £47bn. Last week at the shadow cabinet, we talked about [how] we will need to go further.

“The rate at which the economy is deteriorating, as well as our ambition to cut more taxes, means that we will have to find further savings, and I’m up for that in my department. I know there are areas that we can make savings, and that’s true of every every part of government.”

He added: “There is a moral mission to get our economy growing, give people opportunity, as well as let people keep more of what they earn. It’s pretty simple. We’re Conservative, this is what we stand for.”

A Tory spokesperson acknowledged the party was seeking to make cuts beyond what it had already announced.

“Under Kemi Badenoch’s leadership, the Conservatives have consistently advocated for a smaller state and a government that does fewer things but better,” the spokesperson said.

“In Birmingham , we will go further, setting out further savings to Labour’s bloated welfare bill and cracking down on wasteful spending as part of our plans to build a stronger economy and a stronger country.”

Kemi Badenoch has previously outlined how the government would cut government spending by £47bn, mainly by cutting welfare spending for all non-British or EU citizens.

The plans would also save £8bn by cutting 132,000 civil service jobs, another £1.6bn by scrapping almost all of Labour’s clean energy scheme and more than £7bn by cutting international aid.

In August she promoted Griffith, who previously worked as chief operating officer for Sky, from his role as shadow business secretary.

In government, Griffith worked in the Treasury under Kwasi Kwarteng and was one of the ministers tasked with defending the mini-budget even as the markets tanked in response.

On Friday Badenoch promised another £4bn of spending reductions, including taking another £2.5bn out of the aid budget – leaving it with just £1bn as year – as well as reducing the budget of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport by £1bn.

The Tory leader said she would use half of those savings to pay for an additional 50,000 prison places. She has previously promised to use half of any cuts she makes to reduce the deficit.

Griffiths’ leaked comments come as the Tories prepare to gather in Birmingham for their annual conference, with Badenoch seeking to make a virtue of the growing distance between Labour’s plans for government and her own.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has promised a series of potentially expensive interventions, including a new national care service and public control over utility companies, as he seeks to end what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism”.

However, Badenoch, who has called Margaret Thatcher her hero, is attempting to gain an electoral advantage with her vision of lower taxes and a significantly smaller state.

“[Thatcher] is somebody who brought a lot of wealth and prosperity to this country,” the Tory leader told ITV Meridian on Friday.

“Privatisation was a success … I don’t think that Andy Burnham running the water companies is the answer to those problems.”

The Tories remain in third place in the polls, behind Labour and Reform UK, although Badenoch’s personal ratings have rallied over the last 12 months.

stories.title: Burnham must remember: more regulation is not the best way to improve public services | Phillip Inman

stories.body:
In the NHS as in the private sector, the measure of success should be customer satisfaction and not just box-ticking

Andy Burnham said he wanted to “rewire” the economy. Then he seemed to slam on the brakes, kicking most reforms into the 2030s.

Local government reorganisation is on hold, along with an overhaul of the much-maligned water industry. Social care and significant welfare reform are matters to be resolved by the next government.

A delay is understandable when the issues are knotty and plans on the left to replace the word “rewire” with “renationalise”, stir up accusations of taking Britain back to the 1970s. And yet delay is unnecessary when the knowledge is available now to get on with the kind of changes that rebuild public trust in time for a 2029 election.

There are oblique ways of achieving success, and the measure of success should be customer satisfaction. Without this aim, the hopes of reform are lost.

The economist Sir John Kay, a fellow of St John’s College, Oxford and former head of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, is a keen advocate of organisations that remember for whose benefit they exist. That means their primary aim should be to achieve customer satisfaction. In the private sector, profits will follow. In the public sector, there will be savings.

In his book Obliquity , Kay shows how those companies that pursued shareholder value as their primary aim failed. And those that wanted to produce the best product secured long-term success.

Just as a devotion to shareholder value – a financial metric of the benefit to investors -proved a blind alley for thousands of now-deceased companies, so the reliance on protocols in the public sector as a substitute for understanding the task in hand leads to failed outcomes and wasted money.

You can see it now in the NHS, where satisfaction levels are rising in relation to GP and hospital visits. The new system for booking appointments has its drawbacks, but people are finding doctors are available more quickly, especially for GP and outpatient appointments.

You can see the failures in the NHS from the cover-ups by maternity unit managers of rising mortality rates.

Neither the success nor the failure can be attributed to the regulation of the health service. Regulation is an extra layer of cost that has, time after time, been shown to undermine productive behaviour, either because private providers and managers find they can game the system or it stifles innovation.

Another example can be found in two unconnected government agencies. Last week, the Environment Agency said it would fund the planting of half a million trees, giving funds to councils and mayors and other government bodies to carry out the work. Surely this is a good thing?

On the other hand, you might think it a complete waste of time and money when National Highways, the main road builder in England, planted 850,000 saplings in 2020 along a widened stretch of the A14 north of Cambridge, only to report three years later, in an internal review, that three-quarters of them had died .

These failures are about the way public sector departments and agencies go about their work. Regulation only adds to a tick-box culture that asks: “Did you follow the protocol? If so, everything’s fine.”

Eminent figures in Whitehall, from the former mandarin and Bank of England deputy governor Sir Jon Cunliffe to the House of Lords industry and regulators committee believe the answer is more intensive oversight.

after newsletter promotion

Kay has many examples of companies that grew because the boardroom was dominated by people who were more obsessed about delivering the best service or product than rewarding their shareholders as the chief metric. Profits and improvements in things such as market share were not the dominant metrics in companies that expanded.

The aircraft maker Boeing succeeded before it lost its way chasing quarterly profit targets. ICI, once the UK’s largest industrial company, was broken up and faded away after a higher stock market value became the main target.

The management consultant John Seddon, whose Vanguard consulting firm has adapted the Toyota systems method, supports Kay’s studiously well-informed analysis of what it takes to make a successful organisation. Seddon puts flesh on the bones with the kind of practical systems approach that has helped Portsmouth city council’s housing department win international awards for its repairs service.

He has seen many new initiatives in public sector management from grand strategies to more prosaic schemes for benchmarking services against the private sector. All have failed to improve services.

Seddon is not in favour of ditching regulation altogether . Regulation based on how well an organisation achieves the purpose will, he says, avoid the persistent problem of regulation “running behind events, shutting the stable door after another horse has bolted”.

He adds: “Having a clear statement of purpose will enable regulators to apply sanctions immediately if and when an organisation is found to be undermining its allotted purpose.

“It is time to liberate public servants from the prison of suspicion and distrust that our current method of regulation locks them in, demeaning their professionalism and casting them as part of the problem rather than as active creators of solutions.”

Burnham’s staff should avoid letting the debate about ownership dominate – ignoring a maxim that says “private bad, public good.”. They should work more closely on how public sector organisations achieve better outcomes. The evidence is available. They don’t need to look very far.

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth told Prime Minister Andy Burnham "do not undermine Wales"

Published 1 October 2026

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth has demanded a "new deal" for Wales from the UK government that would put the country on an equal footing with Scotland.

In a letter he said powers over policing, justice, rail and the Crown Estate should be transferred to Cardiff.

Speaking at Plaid Cymru's conference in Llandudno, the party's leader said Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised him he would not undermine Wales.

Ap Iorwerth is expected to meet the prime minister, along with the first ministers of Scotland and Northern Ireland, at the end of the month.

The UK government said it was "committed to building a stronger and fairer Wales in a stronger and fairer United Kingdom".

Plaid Cymru is gathering in Llandudno's Venue Cymru for the first time since it won a historic victory at the Senedd election in May .

The party had won power for the first time, ending Labour's 27 year control of the Welsh government.

Ap Iorwerth said the result amounted to a "new dawn" for Wales, and "the beginning of our work to give flight to a nation whose wings have been clipped for far too long."

But he warned that the upcoming Welsh government budget process would be "tough", and said he would have to "find savings where we can".

Ap Iorwerth has demanded a "new deal" for Wales from the UK government

The Plaid leader said his meeting with Burnham at the Commonwealth Games "did leave me feeling positive - here we had an experienced devolutionist who wanted to bring power and people closer together.

"But as the weeks went on, it became increasingly clear that the prime minister's wave of new powers risked crashing against Offa's Dyke."

He accused Burnham of having a "devolution programme for England".

Speaking to party activists, ap Iorwerth said: "I've looked him in the eyes and said do not undermine Wales as a nation. Do not bypass our Senedd. And he looked me in the eyes and promised he would not. I will hold him to that."

Scotland's government and parliament has more control over the country's own affairs than Wales, where policing and justice are controlled in Westminster, and not Cardiff, and where rail is largely devolved.

Ap Iorwerth said his proposed "new deal" would "redress the historic unfairness of our fiscal and constitutional settlement and put Wales on an equal footing with Scotland as a bare minimum".

"It remains my hope that the prime minister will listen in a shared spirit, and that he'll see that the respect agenda between the Welsh and UK governments must work both ways," he said.

"If he fails, Wales will know again that our best interests will never be served by Westminster, and that it matters little whether who lives in Number 10 Downing Street is an Evertonian or an Old Etonian."

Ap Iorwerth has sent a 2,000 word letter to Burnham spelling out his requests.

Rhun ap Iorwerth became first minister after Plaid Cymru won the Senedd election in May

Plaid Cymru won the largest number of seats at May's election , and since the defection of Sarah Cooper-Lessad it has 44 in the Welsh Parliament chamber.

It is five short of a majority, and needs the help of at least one other party group to pass its spending plans next year . It has been in talks with Labour, the Tories and Reform.

Ap Iorwerth acknowledged a "difficult economic and fiscal backdrop" and said it would be a "tight budget".

"There will be difficult decisions. The budget arithmetic requires us to be disciplined and resourceful."

He added there was a need for a "serious and collaborative approach with other parties".

"We'll have to drive efficiency, improve productivity and find savings where we can; through consolidating and streamlining services, avoiding duplication and focusing on outcomes."

But he said that had to be "free of the damaging approach of the parties on the right", accusing them of defining "savings" and waste by "ideology".

He said the UK government's forthcoming autumn budget was a chance to "reverse the planned-real terms cuts" to the Welsh government's own spending.

Plaid has long-called for Wales to receive substantial extra funds for rail. Ap Iorwerth said that should come "now, not the 2030s".

In another attack on rivals, he asked "others in sincerity to consider whose side they are on".

"Whose side are they on when it comes to protecting Wales from the poison of the far-right," he said.

Firefighters had been tackling wildfires for weeks across Wales over the summer, including this one at Llanwonno Mountain above Ferndale

The party leader paid tribute to fire services who fought the summer's wildfires , and said he would "not allow my government to burden my children and your children with the destructive legacy of complacency on climate change".

He said they had provided an "immediate cash injection to prioritise the longest NHS waits", and had moved "quickly to begin the rollout of the most generous childcare offer anywhere in the UK".

The party eventually plans to roll out childcare to children as young as nine months before the next election.

The first minister said his government was "determined" to tackle problems in the NHS, saying "too many aspects of the service are unfair on patients and on our brilliant staff" and are "unsustainable for the future", although he acknowledged he could not change the NHS "overnight".

He said he would not "shy away" from tackling child poverty "because of a difficult economic and fiscal backdrop".

Labour's Burnham has promised to end triple lock for pensions from 2030 to fund a new national care service. The idea appeared to win praise from Plaid ministers on Friday.

Social care is the responsibility of the Welsh government, and how it spends its money is up to its ministers. Both Plaid and Burnham would face elections before the policy would come in.

Plaid Cymru promised to "make progress" on delivering a national care service in its manifesto for the Senedd election.

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast , the Plaid leader suggested that he may spend extra funds that come to the Welsh government, if any came as a result of more social care in England.

Ap Iorwerth said Burnham's policy was a "good direction of travel", but he added: "We don't know what the consequentials will be."

At a conference fringe, the deputy minister for social care, Delyth Jewell, said Burnham's announcement was "very brave" and that a Plaid Cymru Welsh government would "have to work with the UK government on this".

But she said the building blocks were already being put in place in Wales.

The leaders of the SNP, Plaid Cymru and Sinn Féin met in Cardiff last month

Burnham had previously said he would be "open" to the idea of giving the Welsh government control over policing.

He has also said : "I have to respect the governments in the nations of the UK, and I will, and give a fair hearing to anything that is put to me."

A UK government spokesperson said: "This government is committed to building a stronger and fairer Wales in a stronger and fairer United Kingdom.

"That's why our focus is now on working with the Welsh government to empower local leaders and communities to deliver good growth and jobs in every postcode."

stories.title: Tories aim to be election-ready ahead of party conference
stories.summary: The party will focus on the economy and welfare, as Kemi Badenoch tells her team to prepare for a possible early election.

stories.body:
Leader Kemi Badenoch will focus on the economy at her party's annual conference

Published 2 October 2026

When Kemi Badenoch arrived for her first Conservative conference as leader last year, a member of her entourage overheard somebody wonder aloud: "Who's that?"

This baffled member of the public was actually working at the Conservative conference. Badenoch had been the party's leader and the leader of the opposition for almost a year.

It is an anecdote which underlines the scale of the challenge Badenoch faced at that conference, an event her allies are now with distance willing to acknowledge was make or break for her leadership.

And it is an anecdote which also underlines that, far from break her, that conference represented the start of a major turnaround for Badenoch.

Twelve months on, Badenoch will arrive in Birmingham this weekend in total command of a party whose leading lights are beginning to permit themselves the occasional flicker of optimism after years of misery preparing for, and then experiencing, a brutal election defeat.

Yet for all that Conservatives now believe their leader is an electoral asset, they still face an existential threat from Reform UK and the challenge of how to adjust their strategy to face a new prime minister, Andy Burnham.

The answer to both those issues for Badenoch is a focus on the economy. "Stronger economy, stronger country" will be the party's conference slogan, with the two speeches Badenoch gives - one on Sunday, the other on Wednesday - building on announcements she has made in the past two weeks about cutting benefits for the long-term unemployed.

'Traditional left-right split'

Welfare spending is increasingly seen by the Conservatives as a core battleground with Labour.

During Labour conference they derided the event as the "Welfare Party Conference". Whereas Sir Keir Starmer sought to cut welfare spending before backing down in the face of a rebellion by his own MPs, Burnham has made clear that he believes the way to reduce the benefits bill in the long-term is more up-front investment in support for those out of work.

This is a clear ideological difference which both parties are happy to embrace. Conservative strategists believe there is a broader lesson there.

"The differences between the parties have been quite muddled for a while," one says. "Now that Burnham is prime minister we have a more traditional left-right split."

Another area where Badenoch will embrace that divide in the coming days is the pensions triple-lock .

The policy currently guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% – whichever is the highest.

Badenoch will make clear that the Conservatives continue to support that policy in its current form, breaking with some generally supportive think tanks and policy experts who believe Badenoch should follow Burnham's lead.

In his conference speech on Tuesday , Burnham set out plans to end the existing triple lock from 2030, so the state pension increases at least by inflation or 2.5% - but remove the automatic annual link with average earnings.

The Conservatives hope the sharpening left-right split leaves Reform UK in a strategic bind, occupying a less obvious place on that spectrum.

A year ago some senior Conservatives feared being usurped by Reform as the leading party of the right was a near-inevitability, but now they are optimistic that Nigel Farage's party is on an inexorable slide.

That bullishness is fuelled in large part by the difficulties Reform has faced over Nigel Farage's £5m gift from Christopher Harborne and the fallout - including a police inquiry - from the recent Channel 4 News investigation.

"I find more and more voters raise concerns about Reform with me - people who weren't previously giving us the time of day," one MP said.

"These are successful people with big garages and good jobs who do not necessarily pay that much attention but want a small-c conservative government.

"They were switching to Reform because they were fed up with us and thought Farage was now the main option on the right. But they are starting to come back."

Others are less positive, pointing out that Reform still often record higher shares than the Conservatives in the polls — and more importantly have now won far more votes than them in successive years of local and national elections.

Conservatives pledge 'tough love' benefit rules for under-25s Published 2 days ago

Tories would prevent long-term jobless spending benefits on alcohol and cigarettes Published 24 September

Whether or not there is indeed a long-term trend of the Conservatives regaining ground at Reform's expense, Badenoch may not have long enough to wait.

She has told her team to prepare for this conference as if it is the last before the general election. While not all of her aides agree, Badenoch is convinced that Burnham will go to the polls within the next year.

Party high command started weekly election planning meetings shortly after Burnham succeeded Starmer.

Neil O'Brien, a member of Badenoch's shadow cabinet, has begun work on a manifesto alongside the party's head of policy. It is intended to be a more concise set of pledges than the usual sprawling manifestos.

Also with an eye to the election, the Conservatives will present new faces at the conference who have applied to be candidates at the next election.

Badenoch's ambivalence in some cases, and opposition in others, to ex-MPs who lost their seats in 2024 standing for the party again has attracted some controversy, especially when it comes to the high-profile former cabinet ministers Grant Shapps and Penny Mordaunt.

The leader's supporters are unrepentant, arguing that the party "needs to show we have changed".

Things have certainly changed since last year, at least. That may prove the easy part.

stories.title: US pressures Europe to release diesel reserves as Trump threatens export ban
stories.summary: President Donald Trump has threatened to ban diesel exports in a bid to ease prices in the US ahead of the November elections.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 1 October 2026

Donald Trump has said he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves as he considers banning US exports of the fuel.

The president's comment comes after diesel prices hit record highs on UK forecourts this week, as the Iran war continues to put pressure on the supply of refined fuels.

The UK is heavily reliant on imported diesel from the US. But with US voters also facing higher fuel costs ahead of the midterm elections in November, Trump has threatened to restrict diesel exports .

The UK has been discussing the US supply threats with the EU which is holding a meeting on Friday on the issue.

Banning exports would flood the US market with diesel, and could bring prices down significantly for American drivers.

But experts warn such a ban would put further pressure on diesel prices in other countries, unless they can access further supplies.

The US is a vital supplier of diesel to the world, exporting between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels per day, with most of it going to Latin America.

European countries including France, the Netherlands and the UK, also import a significant amount from the US following the reduction in Russian and Middle Eastern sources of diesel.

Russia's invasion of Ukraine led to sanctions, diverting Russian sales away from Europe. More recently Ukrainian attacks on Russian refining capacity has had a knock-on effect on global supply.

The US-led war on Iran has constrained the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel from that region.

On Thursday, Trump was asked whether he would call on European countries to release some of their own diesel reserves.

"We may do that. They have some diesel," he said.

An earlier post from US Treasury Scott Bessent on social media urged Europe to get ready to release some of their own diesel supplies immediately, arguing that US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.

Diesel prices in the UK hit record highs this week and are hovering just under 200p per litre, according to motoring organisation the RAC.

Over half of the UK's diesel is imported, with 31% of the imports coming from the US.

The Netherlands and Belgium together provide more than a third of UK diesel imports.

UK Energy Minister Martin McCluskey was on a call with European counterparts on Thursday to discuss the potential ban.

A source familiar with the discussions told the BBC it was prudent to prepare a co-ordinated response with other countries, including those across EU, but added that there were still European reserves left from a coordinated release of strategic fuel stocks earlier in the year.

"We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry," a government spokesperson said.

The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages, though prices are expected to rise further.

What a US diesel export ban could mean for you Published 5 days ago

International Energy Agency rules say member states, including the UK, must hold oil stocks equivalent to 90 days of net oil imports.

EU rules say member must hold reserves to cover 61 days of domestic consumption. In total the EU holds nearly 109 million tons of emergency crude and fuel stocks, with around a third in diesel and related fuel products.

A European Commission spokesperson said that there were "lots of calls, lots of meetings" taking place on the diesel situation, including with "high level contacts" in the US administration.

Potentially adding to the pressure on the global diesel market, Chinese refiners have reportedly halted October exports of some fuel products as Beijing prioritises domestic supplies.Prices of petrol and diesel globally have skyrocketed since the outbreak of the US-Israel war in Iran in February. The closure of the vital Strait of Hormuz, which typically transports around a fifth of the world's oil and gas, has pushed up the price of products made from oil.

An export ban from Russia, also a major supplier of diesel, has added to the pressure on prices.

Trump has argued that keeping any surplus barrels of diesel in the US would lower pump prices domestically, offering immediate relief to drivers, truckers, and businesses ahead of the midterm elections.

But David Fyfe, chief economist at Argus Media, said cutting off American supply would be likely to cause international prices to skyrocket.

Diesel prices have hit an all-time high in the UK, with the latest RAC figures showing average pump prices at 199.79p per litre, up from 142.38p

Diesel is harder to refine than gasoline and, because it is used by the haulage industry and in agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

The UK has four refineries which produce more than enough petrol to meet demand, they do not make enough diesel to meet the country's needs.

There were 15.1 million diesel vehicles on UK roads at the end of June, according to the Department for Transport. That is a drop from 15.7 million a year before.

There were 9.8 million diesel cars, down year on year from 10.4 million.

Clarification 2 October: An earlier version of this article said that the governing board of the International Energy Agency (IEA) would meet today (Friday). That sentence was removed after the IEA issued a statement clarifying that no such meeting was planned and it had been announced "erroneously'" by a European Commission spokesperson.

stories.body:
Borrowing can be good, there is no such thing as the ‘nation’s credit card’, and, yes, you can buck the markets – as previous governments have shown

A ndy Burnham does a nice line in nostalgia. His first party conference speech as prime minister was full of fond memories for the Britain of the 1950s and 1960s, when working-class families could sense their lives steadily getting better. The underlying message of his address was that, given time, he could rekindle that optimism and return the country to how it was before Margaret Thatcher wrecked everything.

Much of what Burnham says is true. The 1980s was a decade of deindustrialisation, asset-stripping and financial deregulation that has shaped modern Britain – and not in a good way.

But listen a bit more closely to the speech and it becomes clear that Burnham is struggling to find a way to turn back the clock. For a start, he might not be given time. Energy bills are forecast to rise sharply this winter . John Healey’s first budget, in less than a month’s time, is expected to raise taxes or cut spending – taking money out of an economy that is already struggling.

There’s no question that Burnham and Healey would prefer not to be taking these actions but feel they have no choice. Burnham may well rail against 40 years of neoliberalism. He may think neoliberalism was a dud. But his government is constrained by neoliberal ideas and the language used to express them. Burnham and Healey would never use this language themselves, but that’s irrelevant. To make a real difference, they need to tackle head-on the nostrums of the past four decades. Otherwise they will be for ever in thrall to them.

Top of the list is the idea that the UK government is no different from a household. That means it should match its spending to its income as closely as possible, borrowing prudently and within tightly defined limits. Otherwise it will “max out the nation’s credit card” and risk spiralling into unsustainable debt.

This analogy has the benefit of sounding like a statement of the obvious to many voters, but is actually entirely false. There is no such thing as the nation’s credit card, and a country that prints its own currency can never “max out” or face bankruptcy in the way an individual can.

The notion that the government is living well beyond its means is convenient for those on the political right who have an aversion to public spending. The reality is that, as John Maynard Keynes once said : “Anything we can actually do we can afford.” It was that mentality that allowed the Attlee government to create the welfare state when debt was running at more than 250% of national income – more than double today’s level. I don’t know whether Burnham has seen the new play about Keynes in London’s West End, but it seems as if he ought to.

By the same token, it makes no sense to talk about “black holes” in the public finances every time the government looks on course to miss its targets for borrowing as set out in its fiscal rules. These rules are treated as totemic when in reality they can be changed at any time – and are ditched altogether when there is a crisis.

Again, the idea of a black hole is a convenient fiction for those with an interest in shrinking the size of the state. As with “maxing out the credit card”, it forms part of the inquisition every time a minister goes on the TV or radio with a new spending measure: “That’s all very well but how are you going to pay for it?”

Burnham is committed to re-industrialising Britain, but to do so he will have to break with the neoliberal convention that it is not the job of the government to pick winners. As the prime minister should point out, China, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea have all built up their manufacturing strength by picking winners, and Britain could do the same. Indeed, the one sector that Thatcher picked out for special care and attention – financial services – has gone from strength to strength. Breaking the taboo on picking winners is central to a successful industrial strategy.

Last but not least, Burnham has to address Thatcher’s famous dictum: you can’t buck the market. A cursory glance back at recent economic history shows that governments buck the market all the time. In 2009, the Bank of England responded to the risk of a second Great Depression posed by the global financial crisis by buying government bonds. This provided money to the banking system while cutting the interest rate – or yield – on bonds. This was bucking the market. In 2020, the then Conservative government spent hundreds of billions on a furlough scheme that paid up to 80% of the wages of workers at risk of losing their jobs during the pandemic. This, too, was bucking the market.

So when Burnham, in his conference speech, harked back to the Britain in the immediate decades after the second world war, he missed out a key part of the reason working people felt things were getting better. Rather than being constrained by fiscal rules, governments were committed to full employment. Capital controls meant that financial markets were tightly controlled.

after newsletter promotion

Before we get too nostalgic, it’s worth remembering that things were far from perfect in the so-called postwar golden age. By today’s standards, growth rates were spectacular, but they lagged well behind those of Germany and France. Even so, managed capitalism certainly delivered more for working people than has been the case in the unmanaged capitalism that has followed.

The postwar status quo has been turned on its head. Then, financial markets were caged to ensure that governments could pursue domestic economic goals. Now, governments are caged and the markets are free. It is a classic case of the tail wagging the dog.

Shifting back to a world where finance is fettered is not going to be easy – but until it happens, governments will remain boxed in. Burnham and Healey will be forced to do things they know will harm the economy because they know any deviation from what is acceptable to the received wisdom risks a backlash from the financial markets.

Some new economic thinking is required, and if ever there were a time for an iconoclast like Keynes, it is surely now. He would certainly have no truck with the wrong-headed economic policies of the past half-century and the seemingly commonsense phrases – such as maxing out the credit card – that have been used to disguise just how nonsensical they are.

All credit to Burnham. His analysis of what has gone wrong has clearly rattled his political enemies. Even so, he risks becoming the nearly man of British politics: the prime minister who asked the right questions but failed to come up with the right answers.

Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

Kevin Warsh’s predecessor had been investigated over cost overruns related to central bank renovation project

The US ⁠justice department is not reopening a criminal investigation into former Federal Reserve chair Jerome Powell ⁠for cost overruns ⁠related ​to the central bank’s building renovation project, a department spokesperson said on Friday.

Attorney general Todd ⁠Blanche – in comments to Bloomberg News , which first reported the development – said he has not ruled out ⁠continuing to look into the project’s oversight and potentially take ​action if evidence of ‌wrongdoing came to ‌light.

The Fed’s inspector general on Wednesday said it found ‌no grounds for a criminal referral or evidence of administrative misconduct tied to the project cost overruns. But its conclusion there was lax oversight drew a fresh call for Powell’s resignation from Donald Trump, who across his two presidencies has been a vociferous critic of Powell.

Powell has remained at ‌the Fed as a governor since stepping down as chair in May.

His successor as Fed chair, Kevin ​Warsh said, on Thursday he would hire an independent auditor to “verify accuracy and compliance” for all of the project’s costs.

Blanche told Bloomberg News that if the new review found any evidence ⁠of criminal wrongdoing, the justice department could investigate.

At his final ​press conference ​as Fed chief in ​April, Powell said he would not leave the ​central bank’s board “until this ‌investigation is well and ​truly over, ​with transparency and finality”.

A Fed spokesperson had no immediate comment on Blanche’s statements.

The case was filed in October 2025 on behalf of the United Automobile Workers (UAW), Communications Workers of America (CWA), and American Federation of Teachers (AFT). The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), Muslim Advocates (MA), and the Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic (MFIA) represent the labor unions. The Court ruled that: "This threat of adverse immigration consequences, under a government whose harsh immigration crackdowns has been heavily publicized and reported on, is certainly enough to 'deter a person of ordinary firmness from the exercise of First Amendment rights.' stories.title: Challengers Approach: Third Party App Stores Arrive to Google Play
stories.summary: If you are an Android user, you may have noticed it already: Google has begun allowing rival, third-party app stores to be distributed through the Google Play Store. And if you are a developer, you may have noticed new options for billing and distributing your apps. For years, Epic Games, maker of games such as Fortnite, has been suing Google, alleging violations of antitrust law. Specifically at issue were Google's restrictions on the distribution of alternate app stores through the Play Store, restrictions on app developers who have little practical choice but to distribute their apps through the Play Store, and Google’s rules governing in-app payments and the fees associated with them. Epic’s challenge ultimately resulted in a court order requiring significant changes to Google’s practices. Among other changes, rival, third-party Android app stores are now allowed to access the Play Store’s catalog and to be distributed through the Google Play Store. Developers also have greater freedom to direct users to alternative payment and distribution options. These changes give users and developers more choices and create new opportunities for competition in the Android ecosystem, breaking the power Google once had over many facets of the app ecosystem. This is a win for competition and antitrust enforcement. But the benefits can extend beyond competition itself—more meaningful choice can also create opportunities for greater freedom of online expression, privacy, and security. With alternate app stores able to compete for Android users, Google no longer has the first and last say on what apps can reach users and on what terms. Developers have more options for reaching their audiences, rather than having a single company’s rules determine the terms of access. More importantly, Android users are no longer trapped in an arrangement of feudal security with Google, where users must depend on the goodwill of a monopolist to protect them and guarantee their safety. If Google does not adequately protect their data or security, Android users can now switch to a competitor that does a better job. And if that competitor fails them, they can choose another. Competition in the app store market therefore means competition not only over which apps are offered, the user experience, and developer fees, but also over privacy and security. stories.title: Court Agrees with EFF: Utah’s VPN Law Demands a Technical Impossibility
stories.summary: When state lawmakers attempt to rewrite how the internet works, users rely on courts to recognize that laws can’t make technical impossibilities a reality. That’s why we were happy to see that a court has blocked Utah’s attempt to outlaw the privacy protections of Virtual Private Networks (VPNs). In a win for digital rights, a federal judge has issued a preliminary injunction blocking Utah’s SB 73, the state’s draconian anti-VPN age verification law . The decision comes as EFF submitted our comments to the Utah Department of Commerce, detailing how forcing platforms to detect and block privacy-preserving tools undermines user privacy and security worldwide while demanding the impossible. What SB 73 Does Signed into law earlier this year , SB 73 attempted to regulate adult websites by requiring them to block VPN users or to identify the physical location of visitors using them or similar tools that mask their network traffic. It even went so far as to prohibit websites from offering instructions on how to use a VPN to bypass these checks. This made Utah, to EFF’s knowledge, the first state in the nation to target the use of VPNs to avoid legally mandated age-verification gates. The Utah federal court halted enforcement of the law's VPN provisions last week, r uling that the law likely violates the U.S. Constitution’s prohibition on passing laws that significantly burden businesses and people outside Utah’s borders. SB 73 burdens the rights of all internet users outside of Utah because it requires adult websites to either know every visiting user’s physical location, and then block those in Utah, or to verify every visitor’s age just in case they might be in Utah. The law’s “actual-location provision in practice requires an entity to perform age verification services for every user visiting its site from any location because the entity would violate the law if even one of those users happened to be obfuscating,” the court wrote. The court essentially ruled that Utah has less-burdensome ways to prevent Utah minors from accessing adult websites than requiring all users in the world to comply with SB 73. Aylo’s lawsuit does not challenge SB 73’s provision prohibiting the websites covered by the law from sharing information about VPNs.
